actions.justification: Mandatory first step: continuous vital sign monitoring is essential for risk stratification in acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. Must be completed within 60 minutes.

Mandatory: Wells score is the standard clinical decision tool for pre-test probability of pulmonary embolism in a patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. Must be completed within 60 minutes.
Mandatory: D-dimer is the key initial lab test to rule out PE in patients with low-to-moderate Wells score presenting with dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. Must be completed within 60 minutes.

Per AHA guidelines, a 12-lead ECG should be obtained within 10 minutes of first medical contact for acute chest pain to evaluate for STEMI or other ECG changes. Also useful in PE workup to identify S1Q3T3 pattern or right heart strain.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. Echocardiogram is indicated to assess for right heart strain, which would support PE diagnosis, and to evaluate for other causes of dyspnea such as pericardial effusion or wall motion abnormalities.

Standard supportive care for a patient with acute dyspnea and suspected PE. Although SpO2 is 98%, supplemental oxygen helps maintain oxygenation and is part of initial management while diagnostic workup proceeds.
Patient with acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and pending workup for PE warrants early pulmonology consultation to assist with diagnosis and management planning.

CT pulmonary angiography is the gold standard diagnostic test for pulmonary embolism, which is the leading working diagnosis given acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. D-dimer has been ordered; if elevated or clinical suspicion remains high (Wells score), CT-PA confirms the diagnosis before anticoagulation.
Chest X-ray should be obtained as soon as possible per AHA guidelines to evaluate for alternative diagnoses (pneumothorax, pneumonia, pleural effusion) and assess baseline cardiopulmonary status.

12-lead ECG should be obtained within 10 minutes per AHA Class I guidelines to rule out STEMI and evaluate for PE-associated findings (S1Q3T3, right heart strain, sinus tachycardia). Although order_ecg is already done, order_imaging_ecg is a distinct available action and should be completed to ensure full ECG workup is documented in the imaging workflow.

ABG is indicated to assess oxygenation, ventilation, and acid-base status in a patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, consistent with possible PE workup. CT-PA and D-dimer are already ordered; ABG provides additional physiologic data (A-a gradient, hypoxemia, hypocapnia).
Lower extremity Doppler ultrasound is recommended as part of PE workup to identify DVT as a source of pulmonary embolism, complementing the CT-PA already ordered.
Echocardiogram can assess for right heart strain, which would indicate hemodynamic significance of suspected PE and guide risk stratification and treatment decisions.
CBC will assess for thrombocytosis (risk factor for PE), anemia, and baseline platelet count prior to anticoagulation therapy.
BMP assesses renal function (important for anticoagulant dosing and contrast clearance), electrolytes, and glucose as part of the workup.
BNP helps risk-stratify PE severity by assessing right ventricular strain/dysfunction, guiding treatment intensity decisions.

Troponin is indicated to assess for right heart strain or myocardial injury in the context of suspected pulmonary embolism (acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain). Not yet ordered per completed actions list.
Coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT) are needed prior to initiating anticoagulation therapy for suspected PE, and to establish baseline coagulation status.
Lactate assessment helps evaluate for tissue hypoperfusion and can assist in risk stratification of PE severity, even in a hemodynamically stable patient.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, with extensive workup already completed including CT-PA, D-dimer, Wells score assessment, and lower extremity Doppler. Given the clinical presentation highly suspicious for pulmonary embolism and that diagnostic workup is underway, empiric anticoagulation is appropriate while awaiting CT-PA results, provided no contraindications exist. Guidelines support early anticoagulation in intermediate-to-high probability PE.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, consistent with suspected pulmonary embolism. With CT-PA, D-dimer, and Wells score already ordered/completed, and anticoagulation initiated, LMWH provides definitive anticoagulation therapy for PE management per guideline recommendations. Patient is hemodynamically stable (BP 120/80, HR 80, SpO2 98%) making LMWH appropriate first-line anticoagulation.

Supportive care with IV fluids may be appropriate to maintain preload in the setting of potential PE, as right ventricular strain can reduce cardiac output. Patient is currently stable but monitoring and supportive hydration is reasonable adjunct therapy.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, consistent with pulmonary embolism. CT-PA has been ordered and anticoagulation initiated with LMWH, but given the clinical picture and pending imaging results, systemic anticoagulation with IV unfractionated heparin may be warranted for closer titration and monitoring, especially if high-risk PE is confirmed or if procedural intervention becomes necessary.

Patient with suspected PE (acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain) has received anticoagulation. CT-PA has been ordered. Interventional radiology consultation is appropriate at this stage to evaluate candidacy for catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy if massive or submassive PE is confirmed, especially given the comprehensive workup already completed.
